turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Fourteen-nine! Really, she exclaimed. One’s address, Mr. Worthing, should be a matter of some permanence, it was clear to her, not a fleeting fancy subject to the whims of a lady who, it appeared, rents a residence rather than possesses it. It suggested a certain… instability of purpose, she inquired, wouldn’t he agree?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He stammered slightly, attempting to explain that it was, after all, a temporary arrangement, she would see. Lady Bloxham was, he clarified, merely letting him use the address while he was, as he put it, establishing himself more firmly, of course.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Establishing himself, did he say? A most convenient phrase, Mr. Worthing, particularly when one is attempting to conceal a deficiency. One trusts that this 'establishment' involves more than a mere renting of rooms and a superficial acquaintance with Lady Bloxham’s dubious circle.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He hastened to assure Lady Bracknell that he really hadn't meant to imply anything untoward, quite the contrary! The establishment, he explained, you see, involved a firm of solicitors, actually, who were handling a rather important matter for him. It was all perfectly respectable, he insisted.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A firm of solicitors, Mr. Worthing? How very… diverting. One trusts that this firm, and this 'important matter,' are not connected with… unfortunate antecedents, for those, she observed, are quite impossible to overlook when considering a gentleman’s suitability for marriage.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen insisted, with a touch of exasperation, that her mother really must consider Mr. Worthing's feelings. She found all this questioning dreadfully embarrassing, and it was terribly important that he felt entirely comfortable; after all, he was to be her husband, and one simply could not marry a man who had been subjected to such… scrutiny.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A firm of solicitors, she remarked, her eyebrows arching with a delicate skepticism. It appears Mr. Worthing possesses a remarkable talent for evasion, though one trusts the firm in question is not a mere fabrication designed to shield him from unpleasant inquiries. Indeed, the details of this 'important matter' would be most illuminating.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Really, Mother, this is becoming quite unbearable! Mr. Worthing is perfectly capable of explaining his affairs, and it's simply dreadful to subject him to this… interrogation. One can hardly expect a gentleman to enjoy being treated as if he were a common criminal!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Miss Fairfax with a cool disdain. A mere fabrication, she inquired, such a suggestion was quite impertinent, though not entirely unexpected from one so recently and, one might add, rather precipitously engaged. It would be most advantageous, Mr. Worthing, she continued, if this 'firm' could provide verifiable documentation of its existence and, naturally, of his involvement with it; one could not, she explained, simply accept assertions at face value, particularly when they concerned a gentleman's background.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Really, Mother, Gwendolen declared, one simply *cannot* continue with this absurd charade! Mr. Worthing had already demonstrated his impeccable character, and frankly, these persistent interrogations were quite damaging to his sensibilities – and, naturally, to hers. It was dreadfully unbecoming, and she hoped that Lady Bracknell would consider letting him proceed without further… indignity.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: It appears Miss Fairfax's sensibilities are easily wounded, which, while perhaps endearing, does not entirely absolve her from the necessity of observing decorum. One must, Mr. Worthing, demonstrate a certain resilience to the rigours of society, and frankly, a gentleman of prospects should not be so readily distressed by a few perfectly reasonable inquiries into his lineage.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He felt a blush creep up his neck, and hastened to assure Lady Bracknell that, of course, verifiable documentation could be provided, if she would only permit him the opportunity to retrieve it. It was, he explained, all quite straightforward, really, and he wouldn’t want her to think he was attempting to be… evasive, as she so aptly put it. He simply hadn't anticipated the need for such… formal proof, at this juncture.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing's haste to assure her that documentation *could* be provided only served to confirm her initial suspicions. It is, she observed, a most unfortunate habit to speak of straightforwardness when one is clearly attempting to conceal something. One trusts, of course, that this 'documentation' will not prove to be of a decidedly… unpleasant nature.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He stammered slightly, hoping to regain some semblance of control, and assured Lady Bracknell that the documentation was, in fact, entirely above reproach. It concerned, he hastened to add, a rather… unusual circumstance, but certainly nothing to cause alarm. He truly believed, he insisted, that once she had examined it, she would find everything perfectly satisfactory.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A 'rather unusual circumstance,' Mr. Worthing? Such vagueness is, frankly, most unsettling. One finds oneself compelled to inquire: is this 'unusual circumstance' of a nature to reflect upon the family name, or, indeed, upon the prospects of a young lady of quality who might, under regrettable circumstances, find herself connected to it?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He really hadn't anticipated… well, anything quite like this, did he? It was a most peculiar situation, certainly, and involved a handbag, a railway station, and a most unfortunate misunderstanding, but he was quite confident, absolutely certain, that Lady Bracknell would, upon closer inspection, see how utterly harmless it all was.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell expressed profound disbelief. A handbag, she inquired, Mr. Worthing? A railway station? Really! She found herself quite at a loss. It appeared his narrative was rapidly descending into the realm of the utterly preposterous, and she must confess, Gwendolen’s attachment to such a gentleman was becoming increasingly… perplexing.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Really, Mama, one *does* find it rather tiresome to listen to these endless interrogations! Mr. Worthing is perfectly satisfactory, and Gwendolen knows what she wants, naturally.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing with a look of profound disapproval. Really, the audacity of this young man, attempting to present a narrative involving handbags and railway stations as a matter of consequence! One might as well expect a cucumber sandwich to spontaneously combust.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He stammered slightly, attempting a reassuring smile. Surely, Lady Bracknell, it wasn't *so* very dreadful, really; it was just a rather unfortunate series of events, and he was perfectly prepared to explain everything, every tiny detail, if she would only allow him the opportunity.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen informed Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell remarked that Gwendolen was not engaged to anyone and explained that an engagement should come as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, and that she or Gwendolen’s father would inform her of the fact. She added that it was hardly a matter for her to arrange for herself and then announced that she had a few questions to put to Mr. Worthing, instructing Gwendolen to wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen protested to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell instructed Gwendolen to go to the carriage.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell repeated her instruction for Gwendolen to go to the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen acknowledged Lady Bracknell’s instruction.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell invited Jack to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack thanked Lady Bracknell but stated that he preferred standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell explained that she felt bound to tell Jack that he was not listed among the eligible young men, though she shared the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. She added that she was ready to enter his name if his answers were what a mother required and then inquired whether he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack admitted that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her pleasure, stating that a man should always have an occupation and that there were too many idle men in London. She then asked him how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack replied that he was twenty-nine years old.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell commented that it was a very good age to be married and stated that she believed a man who desired to get married should know either everything or nothing, asking him which he knew.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack responded that he knew nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her pleasure, stating that she did not approve of anything that tampered with natural ignorance and that ignorance was like a delicate exotic fruit. She continued by criticizing modern education and suggesting that it would be dangerous to the upper classes. Finally, she asked about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stated that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell inquired whether the income was in land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack clarified that it was chiefly in investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell observed that land had ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure and that it only provided position. She then asked about a country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack explained that he had a country house with fifteen hundred acres attached, but that he did not depend on it for his income, adding that the poachers seemed to be the only ones benefiting from it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell inquired about the number of bedrooms in the country house and then asked if he had a town house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stated that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham, adding that he could get it back at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell expressed that she did not know Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack explained that Lady Bloxham did not go about very much and that she was considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell remarked that age was no guarantee of respectability of character and asked for the number of the house in Belgrave Square.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack replied that the number was 149.
